newsitem.title: USA: WMX selects 2 for board, hires headhunter.
newsitem.headline: WMX selects 2 for board, hires headhunter.

text.p: WMX Technologies Inc said it selected Robert Miller and Steven Rothmeier to serve on its board as independent directors.
The company also said it hired the executive recruiting firm of Heidrick & Struggles to assist it in a search for a new chief executive to be brought in from outside the company.

The largest U.S. waste hauler and handler said Miller, formerly acting chief executive of Federal-Mogul Corp and chairman of Morrison Knudsen Corp, was chosen as a nominee to be put forward at the company's May 9 annual shareholders meeting.
Miller would fill one of two board seats being vacated by former U.S. Senator Howard Baker and Peter Huizenga, both of whom are retiring from the board.
WMX described Miller as "an expert in financial restructuring and corporate reengineering."

Rothmeier was elected to the board effective immediately to fill the vacancy created February 18 by the surprise resignation of WMX chief executive Phillip Rooney. Rothmeier heads Great Northern Capital, a private investment firm.
Rothmeier was formerly chairman and chief executive of NWA Inc and Northwest Airlines Corp.

"These individuals are outstanding corporate executives noted for financial acumen, no-nonsense leadership and experience managing global companies undergoing change," said WMX chairman and acting chief executive Dean Buntrock.

"Along with Paul Montrone, who joined our board in January, they comprise a substantial body of talent that will help guide and accelerate our recently announced strategic initiatives," Buntrock said.
Neither Miller or Rothmeier was on a slate of four individuals proposed earlier as directors for WMX by an investment fund controlled by financier George Soros.

The slate was withdrawn February 20 by the Soros group, which owns a large stake in WMX, after the group said it had received assurance from WMX that it would try to get two new, independent directors elected to the board.
The Soros group had sought the ouster of Rooney as well.

The group, along with other major investors, has been pressuring WMX for months to improve its performance. The company said February 4 it would divest $1.5 billion in assets, cut 3,000 jobs and buy back 50 million shares.
